view.stem: In geometrical optics, which statement correctly defines a light ray?

options.text: A physical beam occupying a region of space with a finite cross-sectional area.
An imaginary directed line representing the direction in which light propagates.
An undirected line marking positions without specifying a propagation direction.
A straight segment joining a source and a receiving point regardless of the actual propagation path.

intent.task: Recognize the geometrical representation of light's propagation direction, distinguishing it from a finite-width physical beam, an undirected position line and an arbitrary endpoint connection.
intent.source_solution: A light ray is an imaginary directed line representing light propagation in geometrical optics. The prose uses incident rays to describe direction and define incidence relative to a normal; this requires a propagation direction, not a line that must itself be visible sideways. A finite-width beam is a different concept, and the definition cannot be replaced by a straight connection between arbitrary endpoints regardless of propagation. The n68 text does not explicitly restate the formal definition: this is the author's independent solution, not a quotation from an unauthorized earlier card or figure.
intent.unit_reason: One single definition task retains the essential distinction instead of splitting the definition's words or sentences into separate clicks.
limitations: Recognizing a definition does not demonstrate independently writing it or constructing a ray path.
The n68 prose uses this term; the formal definition is independently authored and still requires another worker's fidelity check.

rationales.derivation: A physical beam has a finite cross-sectional area. A ray is an ideal geometrical representation of direction, not that finite spatial region.
rationales.misconception: Identify the narrow beam seen in everyday life with an ideal ray, retaining its finite cross section and losing the abstract directional representation.

rationales.derivation: The directed line specifies propagation direction; its imaginary nature distinguishes a geometrical ray from a finite-width physical beam, consistent with the prose's use of rays for incidence direction.
An undirected line cannot distinguish opposite propagation directions along the same path, so it cannot supply the ray's directional information.
rationales.misconception: Keep only the geometrical positions and delete propagation direction, then identify the resulting undirected line with a ray.

rationales.derivation: A straight path may describe propagation in a suitable homogeneous medium, but that special case does not define a ray as an arbitrary connection made without checking propagation.
rationales.misconception: Promote straight propagation in a particular medium into the definition: connect endpoints first and ignore whether light follows the segment.

view.stem: Which statement correctly defines luminous flux?

options.text: Luminous flux received per unit surface area, measured in lux.
Visually effective light accumulated over a time interval, measured in lumen-seconds.
Light-radiation power evaluated according to the eye's visual response, measured in lumens.
Light-radiation power without weighting by the eye's visual response, measured in watts.

intent.task: Define luminous flux as a visually effective rate of light transfer, distinguishing a rate from accumulated light amount, per-area illuminance and unweighted radiant power.
intent.source_solution: Luminous flux is light-radiation power evaluated by visual response, a visually effective amount per unit time measured in lumens. The selected text gives finite-area average illuminance E=Phi/S and one lumen per square metre corresponding to one lux, so flux Phi differs from the area density E. Accumulated light requires time integration; unweighted radiant power in watts is not the photometric flux in lumens. Visual-response wording clarifies the author's definition of the photometric quantity, not an unsupported response function quoted from n68 or a fixed conversion from watts to lumens.
intent.unit_reason: One single task recognizes the complete physical quantity through meaning and dimensions rather than separate clicks on definition words and units.
limitations: Definition recognition does not demonstrate independently writing the definition or measuring luminous flux.
No spectral-response calculation or conversion from watts to lumens is requested; the authorized text supplies no such data.

rationales.derivation: Phi/S gives average illuminance over a finite area, with lumens per square metre corresponding to lux. Dividing by area changes the quantity being defined.
rationales.misconception: Because flux is received on a surface, additionally divide it by the receiving area and misname the resulting area density as flux.

rationales.derivation: Integrating a flux in lumens over time gives accumulated light, adding a time factor to yield lumen-seconds rather than a transfer rate.
rationales.misconception: Multiply the per-unit-time light transfer by its duration but continue calling the accumulated amount a flux.

rationales.derivation: Power expresses transfer per unit time. Evaluation according to visual response gives photometric luminous flux in lumens, consistent with the authorized lumen-to-area relationship.
Radiant power without visual-response weighting is a radiometric quantity measured in watts. Luminous flux is the corresponding photometric quantity measured in lumens.
rationales.misconception: Retain the radiation's energy-transfer rate but drop the visual-response basis, directly equating radiant power in watts with luminous flux.

view.stem: A source emits luminous flux $\Delta\Phi$ into a very small angular region around a selected direction. Its solid angle $\Delta\Omega$, measured in steradians, specifies the region's angular size; luminous intensity $I$ can be treated as approximately constant within it. Which statement correctly defines the intensity in that direction?

options.text: $I\approx\Delta\Phi/\Delta\Omega$: luminous flux per unit solid angle in that direction.
$I\approx\Delta\Phi/\Delta S$: luminous flux per unit receiving surface area.
$I=\Phi_{\mathrm{total}}$: the source's total luminous flux into all directions.
$I=\Phi_{\mathrm{total}}/(4\pi)$: the intensity in every direction for any point source.

intent.task: Recognize directional luminous flux per unit solid angle as intensity, distinguishing it from flux per area, total flux and unconditional use of total flux divided by 4pi.
intent.source_solution: The local definition is dPhi/dOmega in a direction, approximated by DeltaPhi/DeltaOmega in the stated small region of nearly constant intensity. A small element receives approximately E DeltaS; the authorized law E=I cos(alpha)/R^2 and its subtended solid angle, approximately DeltaS cos(alpha)/R^2, independently yield that ratio. The unit is the candela, lumen per steradian. Total flux divided by 4pi gives only a directional average unless the intensity is the same in all directions. Being a point source alone does not supply angular uniformity.
intent.unit_reason: One single complete-definition task retains solid-angle normalization and directionality rather than separate numerator and denominator questions. The small-region condition states the local approximation, not global isotropy.
limitations: Recognizing flux per solid angle does not demonstrate independently constructing an angular region or deriving the local relationship.
The verbal solid-angle explanation and local derivation are independently authored; n68 does not restate the formal definition, and no unseen figure or unauthorized earlier card is used.

rationales.derivation: Locally dPhi=I dOmega. Summing over a small region of nearly constant I gives DeltaPhi approximately equal to I DeltaOmega, hence the stated ratio.
Flux divided by receiving area is average illuminance. Intensity uses the solid angle of emission, not the receiving surface area.
rationales.misconception: Replace the angular region over which flux is emitted with a plane area receiving it, misapplying the Phi/S illuminance definition to intensity.

rationales.derivation: Total flux sums contributions over all directions rather than flux per unit solid angle in one direction, changing dimensions and discarding directional information.
rationales.misconception: Sum flux into every direction and name it the intensity in one direction, omitting angular normalization and directional differences.

rationales.derivation: 4pi is the full solid angle. Dividing total flux by it gives a directional average, equal to every direction's intensity only for uniform emission; a point-source assumption does not ensure that.
rationales.misconception: Confuse negligible spatial extent with a uniform angular distribution, extending the uniform-sphere 4pi relationship to every point source.

view.stem: Consider only direct illumination of a very small plane element by one point source, with an unobstructed path and no absorption or stray reflections. The incidence angle is between the direction from the element toward the source and the illuminated-side normal, from $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$. In each comparison, conditions not stated to change remain fixed. Select all correct statements.

options.text: Doubling the source's luminous intensity toward the element doubles the element's illuminance.
Doubling the distance along the same emission direction while keeping incidence fixed reduces illuminance to one quarter.
At the same position, tilting the element from normal incidence to $60^\circ$ incidence reduces illuminance to one half.
Whenever a source is a point source, its luminous intensity can be treated as the same in every direction.
In the grazing-incidence limit at $90^\circ$, the element's direct illuminance is zero.
Keeping the source-to-element distance fixed makes illuminance unchanged by any reorientation of the element.

intent.task: Judge dependence of local direct illuminance on directional intensity, distance squared and incidence cosine, including the grazing boundary and the distinction between pointlike and isotropic.
intent.source_solution: Local direct illuminance is E=I cos(alpha)/R^2, using the intensity toward the element, source-to-element distance R and incidence relative to the illuminated-side normal. Holding other factors fixed, doubling I doubles E; doubling R along the same source direction with incidence fixed gives one quarter; tilting at the same position from 0 to 60 degrees gives one half; at 90 degrees the projected factor is zero, giving zero direct illuminance. A point source need not be isotropic. Rotating the receiver at one position leaves the source intensity toward that point unchanged but changes cos(alpha). This is not an unconditional claim about large-area averages, reflections, obstruction or absorption.
intent.unit_reason: The statements jointly express the dependence requested by the source. One multiple-selection unit retains all three factors and boundary behavior without mechanically splitting by factor or example count, and the explicit local model does not add uniform angular emission to an arbitrary point source.
limitations: Selecting relationships does not demonstrate independently listing the factors, deriving the law or drawing a projected-area construction.
The angles and ratio comparisons are explicit author illustrations, not new source data; no exact integral of nonuniform illumination over a finite element is requested.

rationales.derivation: With R and alpha fixed, E=I cos(alpha)/R^2 is linear in intensity toward the element, so doubling I doubles E. Doubling electrical power is not asserted to be the same condition.
Along the same emission direction with I and alpha fixed, the new-to-old ratio is R^2/(2R)^2=1/4. Keeping the direction fixed avoids assuming equal intensity in different directions.
At one position, R and the source's intensity toward that point stay fixed. The illuminance ratio is cos60/cos0=1/2.
A point source has negligible spatial extent in the model; this does not constrain its angular emission distribution, so directional intensities may differ.
rationales.misconception: Substitute an angular-distribution condition for the spatial-size condition, inferring uniform directional intensity from a pointlike source.

rationales.derivation: For the ideal small element the grazing projection factor cos90 is zero, hence direct E is zero in this model. This does not assert zero finite-thickness edge illumination or stray light.
Rotating the element at the same position retains R and source intensity toward that point but changes alpha; E therefore varies with cos(alpha) rather than being independent of orientation.
rationales.misconception: Apply the normal-incidence expression I/R^2 to every receiver orientation, dropping the receiving surface's projected-area cosine.
